sweep_summary: Yine (yine1238) is in the catalog as fixed-strict penultimate (StressTyp2 paraphrase of Matteson 1965:21 plus Hanson 2010 sec. 2.4). The search of works with stress or accent in the title has a single item, Parker 1989 'Un análisis métrico del acento en el piro' (ILV Peru Documento de Trabajo 21:114-125), already listed in our bibliography and the only work devoted specifically to Piro/Yine stress. I located its current SIL archive records (entry 30280 for the article, 29888 for the volume; the Glottolog URL with id 23438 is dead and that number now points to an unrelated item) and found that the whole volume is offered as an open PDF (5.75 MB) on entry 29888, but the file sits behind an automated-access block that our network cannot pass (403 loop by automated download, curl_cffi, cloudscraper, headless and headed Chrome with the Turnstile checkbox clicked); an Internet Archive copy exists but web.archive.org is could not be reached by automated download. So Parker 1989 remains unread: access unknown-from-here, priority high (it should settle how the secondary/tertiary alternating pattern in the rule string is to be stated, which Hanson 2010 calls variable; primary penultimate stress is not in doubt). The only text newly read this search of works with stress in the title is Easterday 2019 (open LangSci book, Appendix B p. 491), a secondary compilation that codes Yine as 'Word stress: Yes; Stress placement: Fixed; correlates: pitch (impressionistic)' - consistent with the classification but not a first-hand placement statement, so no new stress statement was found and the catalog's deciding source is unchanged. Records saved and logged in (, +). Recommended follow-up: download from the SIL URL above in an ordinary browser (it is openly downloadable) and read pp. 114-125.org APIs.

new_statements.quote: El acento primario se ubica en la penúltima sílaba, con la excepción, por supuesto, de las palabras monosílabas. En las palabras que contienen por lo menos cuatro sílabas, el acento secundario cae en la sílaba inicial. En las palabras que contienen seis o más sílabas, el acento terciario se colocará en cada dos sílabas después de la sílaba inicial, a excepción de las palabras que contienen un número impar de sílabas. Ningún acento caerá en la sílaba inmediata precedida al acento primario. [...] Por último, nunca se encuentra ningún acento en la última sílaba de una palabra (Halle y Clements 1983:191; Matteson 1965:20-21).
new_statements.translation: Primary stress is located on the penultimate syllable, with the exception, of course, of monosyllabic words. In words containing at least four syllables, secondary stress falls on the initial syllable. In words containing six or more syllables, tertiary stress is placed on every second syllable after the initial syllable, except in words containing an odd number of syllables. No stress will fall on the syllable immediately preceding the primary stress. [...] Finally, no stress is ever found on the last syllable of a word (Halle & Clements 1983:191; Matteson 1965:20-21).

new_statements.relation_note: Placement is identical to the catalog grid (StressTyp2: stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 10010 101010 1010010 10101010 (1 = a stressed syllable)): penult primary, initial stress from 4 syllables up, alternating stresses from the left with the pre-penult clash position unstressed in odd-parity words, and 3-syllable words 010 (Parker: initial secondary only in words of at least four syllables). Adds detail the binary grid does not encode: a three-way degree hierarchy (penult primary > initial secondary > other alternating tertiary), the explicit final-syllable extrametricality and clash-deletion analysis, and that the data are Matteson's (1965:21) words of 1-14 syllables.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level primary stress on the penult (monosyllables trivially stressed on their only syllable); the final syllable is never stressed (analysed as extrametrical). Secondary stress on the initial syllable in words of four or more syllables; tertiary stresses on alternating syllables counted from the left after the initial (left-headed binary feet built left to right); in odd-parity words the stress that would land on the syllable immediately before the primary-stressed penult is suppressed (clash deletion / Prince's no-clash clause), so two unstressed syllables precede the penult. Quantity-insensitive; the analysis is Halle & Clements (1983) trees plus a metrical grid, with data taken from Matteson (1965:21).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: three degrees. Initial syllable carries secondary stress (words of 4+ syllables; formalised as rule (7) 'Aumentar el acento inicial al nivel de pie añadiendo un asterisco en la fila de cola'); tertiary stress on every other syllable after the initial in words of 6+ syllables; the alternating stress adjacent to the primary is deleted in odd-syllabled words ('en las palabras que contienen un número impar de sílabas, dos sílabas átonas preceden al acento primario', p. 115). Examples pp. 114-115, e.g. 14-syllable ta²palu³škana³wathi³mana³numta³natna¹ka.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllables (no penult); final syllable always unstressed in polysyllables; clash suppression before the penult in odd-parity words. No lexical exceptions or weight effects are mentioned. Parker notes Piro is a counterexample to Halle & Clements' convention that degenerate feet are headed (pp. 121-122).
new_statements.identity_note: Parker 1989 treats 'el piro', 'un idioma arawaka que se habla en la región amazónica del Perú' (p. 114), i.e. Yine/Piro [pib] = yine1238; his data are taken wholesale from Matteson (1965:21), so the article describes the same variety Matteson documented rather than new fieldwork. Work 1 (Naturaleza y vida social 1, 1962) is a school manual tagged to Yine [pib] in Glottolog; it was not opened.

audit.reasoning: Coding: fixed-strict, penultimate primary, stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 10010 101010 1010010 10101010 (1 = a stressed syllable) (primary penult; secondary initial; further stresses on odd syllables except the one before the penult). (1) The record carries no quotation of its own; the StressTyp2 passage it rests on is confirmed in, and the Hanson 2010 passage in the the domain quotation field is verbatim at sec. 2.4 pp. 36-37 of the copy consulted. Matteson 1965:21 itself is not yet obtained. (2) The deciding source is a database paraphrase of the 1965 reference grammar. Against Glottolog's list (Matteson 1965 and Hanson 2010 are the two grammars; the phonology items Lin 1997/2005 and Zimmermann 2013 are on syllable/mora structure and vowel deletion, not stress) the best first-hand descriptions are Matteson (1954/1965) and Hanson 2010, plus Parker 1989 as the one dedicated stress paper. (3) downloaded now: Matteson 1954 (open Rosetta excerpt) state

sources.quote: "Primary stress of words occurs on the penultimate syllable, and secondary stress on the first syllable. In words with an even number of syllables a slight stress occurs on all odd-numbered syllables. In words with an odd number of syllables a slight stress occurs on all odd-numbered syllables except the one immediately preceding the primary-stressed penultimate syllable. ... However, in calling and exclamation the stress may be moved to the final syllable with raise of pitch and lengthening of the final vowel."
